title: Proving Our Backend Service Survives a Cassandra Node Failure
excerpt: A local, production-like test showing that the backend keeps serving reads and writes when one Cassandra node is unavailable—and what Node 24 revealed about driver compatibility.
content:
The backend service kept serving reads and writes on a local three-node Cassandra cluster with one node stopped. We proved the failure scenario without changing production code.

## Summary

- **Goal:** Show that the backend survives one Cassandra node going down.
- **Method:** Recreate a production-like topology locally with Cassandra 3.11.19, replication factor 3, and the application running on Node 24.
- **Result:** With three nodes up and with two nodes up, the API returned synthetic application data. Starting the application while one node was already down also worked.
- **Important finding:** `cassandra-driver` 4.6.4 breaks on Node 24 with `util.isDate is not a function`; version 4.8.0 or later fixes it.
- **Misconception cleared:** Removing a host from `contactPoints` does not stop that node. The driver discovers the rest of the cluster after connecting.

## The problem

The service had not been shown to keep working when one Cassandra node was unavailable. A single-node staging environment could not demonstrate this failure mode.

The local test used a three-node cluster, RF=3, consistency `ONE`, authentication disabled, and a data-center-aware round-robin policy. These were test assumptions only; no production or staging environment was accessed or changed.

## Building the local cluster

We used Docker Compose with Cassandra 3.11.19 and three local nodes. The keyspace used `NetworkTopologyStrategy` with RF=3 rather than a single-node strategy. That distinction matters: a three-node cluster only protects data when the keyspace replicates each row across the nodes.

The application ran inside the Docker network using Node 24 so it could reach all local Cassandra nodes. Synthetic test rows were inserted through the application's normal data model and encryption utility; no customer data was used.

## Failure cases tested

The baseline was run with all three nodes up. We then stopped the seed node and repeated the API request with the other two nodes still up. The request continued to return the complete payload.

We also tested stopping a non-seed node, starting the application while a node was down, removing a node from the configured contact points, and restarting the stopped node. In every case the API continued to work, and the restarted node caught up in roughly 10–15 seconds.

## Why the service keeps working

`contactPoints` is only the driver's starting list, not a static allowlist.

1. The driver connects to any available starting address.
2. It reads the cluster topology and learns about the other nodes.
3. It distributes requests using a data-center-aware round-robin policy.
4. It marks unavailable nodes down and routes around them.

With RF=3, each node has a replica. With consistency `ONE`, a read or write needs a response from only one replica, so either surviving node can satisfy the request. A dead starting address matters only if every configured address is unavailable.

## The Node 24 driver issue

The most significant issue was runtime compatibility rather than failover. `cassandra-driver` 4.6.4 uses `util.isDate`, which was removed in Node 23 and later. On Node 24, writes failed with:

```text
util.isDate is not a function
```

The same path worked on Node 20. Driver versions 4.7.1 and 4.7.2 still exhibited the issue; 4.8.0 and later did not. Version 4.8.0 was installed locally for the test, while the declared application dependency was intentionally left unchanged. The resolved version still needs to be checked inside the deployed image.

## Limits and next steps

This was a local topology and failure-mode test, not a production qualification. It did not cover sustained load, latency, two simultaneous node failures, long outages, repair behaviour, or the full customer journey.

Next steps are to verify the resolved driver version in the deployed image, build and test the actual image in CI, expand staging to three nodes with RF=3, and run any production test only during an approved maintenance window. After a prolonged outage, run a repair.

The short version: with RF=3 and consistency `ONE`, the backend continued reading and writing when one of three Cassandra nodes was down.
